lines.text: At twenty to midnight on April 14th, 1912, leading stoker Frederick Barrett was in the Titanic's forward boiler room when water started pouring in through the ship's side.
It came in about two feet above the floor he was standing on.
He ran aft into the next boiler room, and the watertight door came down behind him.
Up on the bridge, First Officer William Murdoch had already pulled the lever that shut those doors.
The system did what it was built to do.
Two hours and forty minutes later, the ship was gone.
The usual explanation is that the walls between her compartments didn't go high enough.
Less than two months later, the Harland and Wolff naval architect who presented the ship's flooding calculations was asked about exactly that, under oath.
The weakness was somewhere else in the design, and a ship launched half a century earlier had already shown what was missing.
Harland and Wolff divided the Titanic's hull with fifteen steel bulkheads, walls running across the ship from side to side, which made sixteen watertight compartments.
The doors through those walls in the boiler and engine rooms could all be closed from the bridge with that one lever.
The shipyard's calculations had her floating with any two neighboring compartments flooded.
At the bow she could take more: the first four could fill and she would still float.
Back in 1891, a Board of Trade committee had recommended two, and even that wasn't compulsory.
At the British inquiry, Harland and Wolff's Edward Wilding testified that the Titanic's safety margin above the water was about twice what that committee had suggested.
